orig_sentences: “The play’s the thing,” says Hamlet, “wherein I’ll catch the conscience of the king.”
“Catch” is indeed the word.
For conscience moves swiftly or withdraws within itself.
It has to be caught on the wing, at that barely perceptible moment when it glances fleetingly at itself.
The everyday man does not enjoy tarrying.
Everything, on the contrary, hurries him onward.
But at the same time nothing interests him more than himself, especially his potentialities.
Whence his interest in the theater, in the show, where so many fates are offered him, where he can accept the poetry without feeling the sorrow.
There at least can be recognized the thoughtless man, and he continues to hasten toward some hope or other.
The absurd man begins where that one leaves off, where, ceasing to admire the play, the mind wants to enter in.
Entering into all these lives, experiencing them in their diversity, amounts to acting them out.
I am not saying that actors in general obey that impulse, that they are absurd men, but that their fate is an absurd fate which might charm and attract a lucid heart.
It is necessary to establish this in order to grasp without misunderstanding what will follow.
mod_sentences: "The play's the thing," declares Hamlet, "wherein I'll catch the conscience of the King."
"Catch" is precisely the right word.
For consciousness moves with extreme speed, or retreats instantly back into itself.
It must be captured mid-flight, at that fleeting, almost imperceptible instant when it casts a backward glance upon its own reflection.
The ordinary person has no patience for lingering self-examination.
On the contrary, the momentum of daily life relentlessly drives them forward.
Yet at the same time, nothing fascinates a person more than themselves—especially their own unrealized possibilities.

Hence their enduring attraction to the theater, to the stage, where countless alternative destinies are laid out before them, allowing them to savor the dramatic beauty without bearing the actual weight of the agony.
In that passive spectator one recognizes the unreflective person, perpetually rushing toward one comforting hope after another.
The absurd man begins precisely where that spectator stops: where, refusing to remain a mere detached observer, the mind demands to enter the arena directly.
To inhabit all these varied human lives, experiencing them in their full multiplicity, is to perform them on the stage.

I am not claiming that actors as a class consciously obey this philosophical imperative, or that they are personally absurd heroes; rather, their professional destiny is inherently an absurd destiny—one capable of fascinating and attracting a lucid mind.
This distinction must be established clearly from the outset to avoid any confusion in what follows.
pairs.move: The Spectator vs. The Actor (Passive Illusion vs. Active Embodiment). Everyday humans use theater as escapism: an effortless peek into alternate lives without personal risk or suffering. The absurd person, however, refuses passive spectatorship. By physically embodying multiple characters, the actor transforms the quantitative appetite of the absurd into physical reality, living multiple lifetimes in an afternoon.

orig_sentences: The actor’s realm is that of the fleeting.
Of all kinds of fame, it is known, his is the most ephemeral.
At least, this is said in conversation.
But all kinds of fame are ephemeral.
From the point of view of Sirius, Goethe’s works in ten thousand years will be dust and his name forgotten.
Perhaps a handful of archæologists will look for “evidence” as to our era.
That idea has always contained a lesson.
Seriously meditated upon, it reduces our perturbations to the profound nobility that is found in indifference.
Above all, it directs our concerns toward what is most certain—that is, toward the immediate.
Of all kinds of fame, the least deceptive is the one that is lived.
mod_sentences: The actor's domain is the kingdom of the fleeting.
Of all forms of celebrity, theatrical fame is acknowledged to be the most ephemeral.
At least, that is the common platitude.
Yet in truth, every form of human glory is ephemeral.
Viewed from the cosmic perspective of Sirius, even Goethe's masterpieces will be reduced to dust in ten thousand years, and his name will be utterly erased.
At most, a few future archaeologists may sift the earth for artifacts of our forgotten civilization.
That realization has always offered a profound lesson.
Contemplated with seriousness, it dissolves our petty anxieties into the dignified nobility of existential indifference.
Above all, it turns our attention toward the only certainty we possess: the immediate present.
Of all varieties of fame, the least deceptive is the fame that is directly experienced in the flesh.
pairs.move: Cosmic Indifference (The Perspective of Sirius). Intellectuals boast of posthumous immortality through books and monuments. Camus invokes the cosmic scale (the star Sirius) to show that all art and human memory will perish. The actor's fame is the most honest because it does not pretend to outlive its performance; it is expended and enjoyed entirely in real time.

orig_sentences: Hence the actor has chosen multiple fame, the fame that is hallowed and tested.
From the fact that everything is to die someday he draws the best conclusion.
An actor succeeds or does not succeed.
A writer has some hope even if he is not appreciated.
He assumes that his works will bear witness to what he was.
At best the actor will leave us a photograph, and nothing of what he was himself, his gestures and his silences, his gasping or his panting with love, will come down to us.
For him, not to be known is not to act, and not acting is dying a hundred times with all the creatures he would have brought to life or resuscitated.
mod_sentences: The actor has therefore chosen an immediate, collective glory—a fame affirmed and experienced night after night before a living audience.
From the undeniable truth that everything must eventually perish, he derives the most rigorous conclusion.
For the actor, success or failure is instantaneous: he either triumphs in the room or he fails completely.
A writer can always nurse the secret hope of future recognition even when neglected in his lifetime, assuming his written pages will testify to posterity on his behalf.

At best, the actor leaves behind a lifeless photograph; nothing of his living essence—his sudden physical gestures, his pregnant pauses, his breath catching in grief or panting with desire—can ever be preserved.
For the actor, not to be recognized in the moment is not to perform at all; and not performing means dying a hundred deaths alongside every character he was poised to ignite into life.
pairs.move: The Binary of the Stage vs. The Delusion of Posterity. The writer can hide behind the illusion of posthumous vindication; the actor cannot. The actor's existence is binary: immediate triumph or immediate oblivion. To be unperformed is to surrender the creation of life.

orig_sentences: Why should we be surprised to find a fleeting fame built upon the most ephemeral of creations?
The actor has three hours to be Iago or Alceste, Phèdre or Gloucester.
In that short space of time he makes them come to life and die on fifty square yards of boards.
Never has the absurd been so well illustrated or at such length.
What more revelatory epitome can be imagined than those marvelous lives, those exceptional and total destinies unfolding for a few hours within a stage set?
Off the stage, Sigismundo ceases to count.
Two hours later he is seen dining out.
Then it is, perhaps, that life is a dream.
But after Sigismundo comes another.
The hero suffering from uncertainty takes the place of the man roaring for his revenge.
By thus sweeping over centuries and minds, by miming man as he can be and as he is, the actor has much in common with that other absurd individual, the traveler.
Like him, he drains something and is constantly on the move.
He is a traveler in time and, for the best, the hunted traveler, pursued by souls.
If ever the ethics of quantity could find sustenance, it is indeed on that strange stage.
mod_sentences: Why should we find it strange that a transient reputation rests upon the most ephemeral of human creations?
The actor is granted exactly three hours to inhabit Iago or Alceste, Phèdre or Gloucester.
Within that brief window, he brings them screaming into existence and escorts them to their deaths across fifty square yards of wooden floorboards.
Never has the condition of the absurd been illustrated with such visceral clarity.
What more vivid microcosm could one conceive than these extraordinary destinies, unfolding from birth to annihilation within the artificial frame of a theatrical set?
Once he steps into the wings, Prince Sigismundo ceases to exist; two hours later, the man who played him is spotted eating supper at a local tavern.
It is at that precise moment, perhaps, that Calderón's maxim rings true: life is indeed a dream.
Yet directly behind Sigismundo follows another persona: the indecisive, agonizing intellectual abruptly replaces the warlord crying out for bloody vengeance.
By traversing centuries and sensibilities, by physically enacting human nature both as it is and as it might be, the actor shares a deep kinship with that other absurd wanderer: the traveler.
Like the traveler, he exhausts his surroundings and remains perpetually in motion.
He is a traveler across historical time—and, at his peak, a hunted traveler pursued by the ghost of a hundred souls.
If the ethic of quantitative experience ever found an ideal laboratory, it is surely upon these strange, illuminated boards.
pairs.move: The Actor as Time Traveler (Calderón's 'Life is a Dream'). On fifty square yards of wooden boards, a complete human destiny is ignited, exhausted, and extinguished within three hours. The actor demonstrates the ultimate quantitative triumph over linear time: by inhabiting conflicting souls in rapid succession, he becomes a traveler through centuries of human consciousness.

orig_sentences: To what degree the actor benefits from the characters is hard to say.
But that is not the important thing.
It is merely a matter of knowing how far he identifies himself with those irreplaceable lives.
It often happens that he carries them with him, that they somewhat overflow the time and place in which they were born.
They accompany the actor, who cannot very readily separate himself from what he has been.
Occasionally when reaching for his glass he resumes Hamlet’s gesture of raising his cup.
No, the distance separating him from the creatures into whom he infuses life is not so great.
He abundantly illustrates every month or every day that so suggestive truth that there is no frontier between what a man wants to be and what he is.
Always concerned with better representing, he demonstrates to what a degree appearing creates being.
For that is his art—to simulate absolutely, to project himself as deeply as possible into lives that are not his own.
At the end of his effort his vocation becomes clear: to apply himself wholeheartedly to being nothing or to being several.
The narrower the limits allotted him for creating his character, the more necessary his talent.
He will die in three hours under the mask he has assumed today.
Within three hours he must experience and express a whole exceptional life.
That is called losing oneself to find oneself.
In those three hours he travels the whole course of the dead-end path that the man in the audience takes a lifetime to cover.
mod_sentences: Exactly how much the actor absorbs internally from the roles he portrays is difficult to measure.
But that psychological question is beside the point.
The real question is how completely he merges his identity with those unrepeatable lives.
Frequently, he carries them with him off the stage, their emotional resonance spilling over the boundaries of the performance.
They linger in his physical presence; he cannot easily sever his own body from the ghosts he has animated.
At dinner, reaching casually for his wine glass, he inadvertently replicates Hamlet's motion of raising the poisoned chalice.
No, the gulf separating the actor from the creatures he breathes life into is remarkably thin.
Day after day, month after month, he provides compelling proof of an unsettling truth: there is no clear boundary between what a human being pretends to be and what they actually are.
Constantly focused on externalizing character through action, he demonstrates how powerfully appearance generates being.
For that is his discipline: to simulate so completely that he projects himself into destinies foreign to his own.
When his labor is finished, his existential calling stands revealed: to devote himself entirely either to being nobody, or to being a multitude.
The tighter the time limit imposed for constructing his character, the more formidable his craft must be.
Within three short hours, he must expire beneath the mask he put on tonight.
In three hours, he must experience, articulate, and exhaust an entire lifetime.
This is the true meaning of losing oneself in order to find oneself.
Across that single evening, he travels the entire trajectory of that fatal, dead-end road which takes the spectator in the seats an entire lifetime to navigate.
pairs.move: Appearance Creates Being (The Dissolution of Fixed Identity). Camus challenges the metaphysical assumption of an essential 'true self.' The actor demonstrates that pretending to be someone physically actually produces that being ('appearing creates being'). The actor compresses into 180 minutes the identical mortal cul-de-sac that the passive spectator takes eighty years to endure.

orig_sentences: A mime of the ephemeral, the actor trains and perfects himself only in appearances.
The theatrical convention is that the heart expresses itself and communicates itself only through gestures and in the body—or through the voice, which is as much of the soul as of the body.
The rule of that art insists that everything be magnified and translated into flesh.
If it were essential on the stage to love as people really love, to employ that irreplaceable voice of the heart, to look as people contemplate in life, our speech would be in code.
But here silences must make themselves heard.
Love speaks up louder, and immobility itself becomes spectacular.
The body is king.
Not everyone can be “theatrical,” and this unjustly maligned word covers a whole æsthetic and a whole ethic.
Half a man’s life is spent in implying, in turning away, and in keeping silent.
Here the actor is the intruder.
He breaks the spell chaining that soul, and at last the passions can rush onto their stage.
They speak in every gesture; they live only through shouts and cries.
Thus the actor creates his characters for display.
He outlines or sculptures them and slips into their imaginary form, transfusing his blood into their phantoms.
I am of course speaking of great drama, the kind that gives the actor an opportunity to fulfill his wholly physical fate.
Take Shakespeare, for instance.
In that impulsive drama the physical passions lead the dance.
They explain everything.
Without them all would collapse.
Never would King Lear keep the appointment set by madness without the brutal gesture that exiles Cordelia and condemns Edgar.
It is just that the unfolding of that tragedy should thenceforth be dominated by madness.
Souls are given over to the demons and their saraband.
No fewer than four madmen: one by trade, another by intention, and the last two through suffering—four disordered bodies, four unutterable aspects of a single condition.
mod_sentences: A pantomimist of the temporary, the actor refines his craft exclusively within the realm of surfaces and appearances.

The fundamental rule of the stage is that the human heart can communicate its internal truth only through physical gesture and the living body—or through the human voice, which belongs equally to the flesh and to the spirit.
The law of the theater dictates that every psychological nuance must be magnified and translated into physical reality.

If an actor were to portray love on stage with the whispered murmurs of everyday life, using the mute glances of private domesticity, his performance would remain an indecipherable secret to the room.
On stage, even silence must ring with audible force.
Passion must speak with heightened volume, and complete immobility must become a gripping spectacle.
The physical body reigns supreme.
Not everyone possesses the talent to be "theatrical"—a word unfairly degraded, which in truth encompasses an entire aesthetic and moral philosophy.
Ordinary human life is spent in hesitation, evasive glances, and stifled silences.
The actor arrives on stage as a radical intruder.
He shatters the paralytic spell binding the human soul, finally letting dormant passions storm the platform.
Here, passions speak through muscular movement; they announce their reality through cries, physical confrontations, and declarations.
In this way, the actor builds figures meant for public exposure.
He chisels their silhouettes, slips into their ghostly contours, and transfuses his own warm blood into their fictional veins.
I am speaking, of course, of classical tragedy—the kind of drama that permits an actor to realize his purely physical destiny.
Consider Shakespeare.
In his visceral theater, raw physical passions orchestrate the entire drama.
They provide the sole engine of the narrative; without them, the architecture falls to pieces.
King Lear would never arrive at his fatal rendezvous with madness on the storm-swept heath were it not for the impulsive, violent gestures with which he disowns Cordelia and banishes Edgar.
It is entirely fitting that this catastrophic collapse should be ruled by lunacy.
Souls are surrendered to chaotic furies and their frenzied dance.

Shakespeare assembles no fewer than four distinct madmen: one a professional fool, one feigning insanity by design, and two driven mad through unbearable anguish—four shattered physical vessels embodying four unspeakable dimensions of a single human condition.
pairs.move: The Primacy of the Body in Drama (Shakespeare's Four Madmen). In normal life, humans hide behind polite restraint and repression. Great theater translates internal suffering into visceral, physical motion. Using King Lear, Camus demonstrates how tragedy operates through bodily violence and physical madness: the abstract mind must yield to the reality of the flesh.

orig_sentences: The very scale of the human body is inadequate.

The mask and the buskin, the make-up that reduces and accentuates the face in its essential elements, the costume that exaggerates and simplifies—that universe sacrifices everything to appearance and is made solely for the eye.
Through an absurd miracle, it is the body that also brings knowledge.
I should never really understand Iago unless I played his part.
It is not enough to hear him, for I grasp him only at the moment when I see him.
Of the absurd character the actor consequently has the monotony, that single, oppressive silhouette, simultaneously strange and familiar, that he carries about from hero to hero.
There, too, the great dramatic work contributes to this unity of tone.
This is where the actor contradicts himself: the same and yet so various, so many souls summed up in a single body.
Yet it is the absurd contradiction itself, that individual who wants to achieve everything and live everything, that useless attempt, that ineffectual persistence.
What always contradicts itself nevertheless joins in him.
He is at that point where body and mind converge, where the mind, tired of its defeats, turns toward its most faithful ally.
“And blest are those,” says Hamlet, “whose blood and judgment are so well commingled that they are not a pipe for fortune’s finger to sound what stop she please.”
mod_sentences: The natural proportions of the naked human frame are almost insufficient for the stage.

The ancient tragic mask and high-soled buskin, the exaggerated makeup that reduces the face to stark archetypal planes, the heavy costumes that dramatize and distill character—this entire world sacrifices inward subtlety to external form, engineered purely for the spectator's eye.
Yet through a strange and marvelous paradox, it is this physical apparatus that delivers genuine comprehension.
I could never truly understand Iago simply by analyzing his speeches; I understand him only when I physically embody him.
It is not enough to read his words; I grasp his malice only when I watch his posture and mimic his gait.

From his absurd existence, the actor inherits a certain underlying monotony: that persistent, singular physical silhouette, at once foreign and intimate, which he drags with him from one legendary role to the next.
In this respect, great classical drama supports this unity of tone.

Here lies the central contradiction of the actor's craft: he remains the identical flesh-and-blood person, yet manifests an astonishing multiplicity of souls gathered inside a solitary physical frame.

This tension mirrors the foundational paradox of the absurd itself: a mortal being longing to experience everything and conquer every fate, locked in a magnificent, futile struggle marked by relentless perseverance.
Contradictory impulses achieve physical reconciliation within him.
He stands at the exact crossroads where intellect and biology fuse—where the mind, exhausted by abstract philosophical defeats, turns back toward its most dependable comrade: the body.
"And blessed are those," Hamlet proclaims, "whose blood and judgment are so well commingled that they are not a pipe for fortune's finger to sound what stop she please."
pairs.move: Embodied Knowledge: Flesh as Epistemology. Theoretical analysis of evil (like Iago's malice) remains an academic abstraction until it is physically performed through breath, posture, and facial musculature. The actor resolves the Cartesian split between mind and matter: the mind, exhausted by unsolvable metaphysical riddles, grounds itself in the living physiology of the body.

orig_sentences: How could the Church have failed to condemn such a practice on the part of the actor?

She repudiated in that art the heretical multiplication of souls, the emotional debauch, the scandalous presumption of a mind that objects to living but one life and hurls itself into all forms of excess.
She proscribed in them that preference for the present and that triumph of Proteus which are the negation of everything she teaches.
Eternity is not a game.
A mind foolish enough to prefer a comedy to eternity has lost its salvation.
Between “everywhere” and “forever” there is no compromise.
Whence that much maligned profession can give rise to a tremendous spiritual conflict.
“What matters,” said Nietzsche, “is not eternal life but eternal vivacity.”
All drama is, in fact, in this choice.
mod_sentences: How could the Christian Church have failed to condemn the actor's vocation?

The Church recoiled from an art that heretically multiplied the singular human soul—denouncing its emotional license and the brazen arrogance of a mind that refuses to content itself with a solitary earthly life, plunging instead into every imaginable excess.
The Church outlawed the actor's adoration of the immediate present and his protean shape-shifting, recognizing in them the absolute negation of everything theology proclaims.
Eternity cannot be treated as a theatrical diversion.
A mind frivolous enough to prefer a three-hour comedy to eternal salvation has forfeited its place in heaven.
Between the horizontal spread of being "everywhere" in time and the vertical absolute of existing "forever," no reconciliation is possible.
Hence this historically reviled profession has constantly generated intense spiritual warfare.
"What matters," Nietzsche declared, "is not eternal life, but eternal vivacity."
The essence of theatrical tragedy resides entirely within that fateful choice.
pairs.move: The Church's Condemnation: 'Everywhere' vs. 'Forever'. The historical excommunication of actors was not an accident of puritanism; it was an ontological clash. The Church demands that man invest everything in vertical eternity ('forever'); the actor invests everything in horizontal richness across mortal time ('everywhere'). The actor embodies Nietzsche's dictum: eternal vivacity over eternal salvation.

orig_sentences: Adrienne Lecouvreur on her deathbed was willing to confess and receive communion, but refused to abjure her profession.
She thereby lost the benefit of the confession.
Did this not amount, in effect, to choosing her absorbing passion in preference to God?
And that woman in the death throes refusing in tears to repudiate what she called her art gave evidence of a greatness that she never achieved behind the footlights.
This was her finest role and the hardest one to play.
Choosing between heaven and a ridiculous fidelity, preferring oneself to eternity or losing oneself in God is the age-old tragedy in which each must play his part.
mod_sentences: On her deathbed, the celebrated actress Adrienne Lecouvreur was willing to make her confession and receive Holy Communion, but steadfastly refused to renounce her acting profession.
By that refusal, she forfeited the Church's absolution.
Did this act not amount, in reality, to choosing her consuming mortal art over the claims of God?
And that dying woman, weeping in her death throes while refusing to disown what she revered as her art, exhibited a tragic heroism she never matched behind the footlights.
That final refusal was her most magnificent performance, and the most agonizing role she ever undertook.

Forced to choose between the promise of paradise and a stubborn, unyielding fidelity to her mortal craft—weighing loyalty to one's own identity against the submission of the soul to God—she enacted the timeless tragedy in which every conscious human being must take a stand.
pairs.move: The Defiance of Adrienne Lecouvreur. By refusing on her deathbed to renounce her stagecraft in exchange for the last rites, Lecouvreur enacted the ultimate absurd revolt. She chose her ephemeral mortal passion over eternal salvation, proving that authentic human dignity lies in unyielding loyalty to one's earthly devotion.

orig_sentences: The actors of the era knew they were excommunicated.
Entering the profession amounted to choosing Hell.
And the Church discerned in them her worst enemies.
A few men of letters protest: “What! Refuse the last rites to Molière!”
But that was just, and especially in one who died onstage and finished under the actor’s make-up a life entirely devoted to dispersion.
In his case genius is invoked, which excuses everything.
But genius excuses nothing, just because it refuses to do so.
mod_sentences: Actors of that era knew beyond doubt that they stood officially excommunicated.
Entering the theatrical profession was tantamount to choosing damnation.
And the Church correctly identified them as its most dangerous philosophical adversaries.
Later literary critics protested with moral indignation: "How barbaric to deny Christian burial to Molière!"

Yet the Church's judgment was entirely consistent—especially toward a playwright who collapsed upon the stage itself, concluding beneath greasepaint and costume a life dedicated entirely to the dispersion of the self into temporary roles.
Admirers appeal to Molière's genius as an all-forgiving defense.
But true genius seeks no special dispensations, precisely because it accepts the full consequences of its defiance.
pairs.move: Molière Dying in Greasepaint. Denying Christian burial to Molière was logically just: Molière died onstage in the middle of performing The Hypochondriac, literally dying under actor's greasepaint. He gave his entire life to the ephemeral dispersion of the self. True artistic genius demands no theological pardons; it stands by its choice of the mortal over the divine.

orig_sentences: The actor knew at that time what punishment was in store for him.
But what significance could such vague threats have compared to the final punishment that life itself was reserving for him?
This was the one that he felt in advance and accepted wholly.
To the actor as to the absurd man, a premature death is irreparable.
Nothing can make up for the sum of faces and centuries he would otherwise have traversed.
But in any case, one has to die.
For the actor is doubtless everywhere, but time sweeps him along, too, and makes its impression with him.
mod_sentences: In those days, the actor was fully aware of the ecclesiastical penalties awaiting him.
Yet what terrifying weight could such supernatural warnings carry when weighed against the final, inescapable penalty life itself had prepared for him?
It was this inevitable mortal finish that he anticipated from the beginning and embraced without reservation.
To the actor, as to every absurd individual, an untimely death represents an irreparable disaster.
Nothing can compensate for the lost sum of human faces, roles, and centuries he would otherwise have brought to life.
Yet regardless of when it strikes, death remains inescapable.
For while the actor seemingly travels everywhere across the imaginative expanse, linear time sweeps him along just as inexorably, leaving its relentless scars upon his flesh.
pairs.move: Untimely Death as Irreparable Loss. The absurd man fears neither hell nor moral judgment; his only real adversary is premature physical death. In an ethic of quantity, every year or decade lost is an absolute subtraction from the sum of potential experiences, characters, and eras that could have been lived.

orig_sentences: It requires but a little imagination to feel what an actor’s fate means.
It is in time that he makes up and enumerates his characters.
It is in time likewise that he learns to dominate them.
The greater number of different lives he has lived, the more aloof he can be from them.
The time comes when he must die to the stage and for the world.
What he has lived faces him.
He sees clearly.
He feels the harrowing and irreplaceable quality of that adventure.
He knows and can now die.
There are homes for aged actors.
mod_sentences: It requires only a small leap of imagination to grasp the ultimate meaning of an actor's destiny.
It is within the crucible of time that he invents and tallies his diverse roles.
It is within time, equally, that he learns to master and inhabit them.
The greater the multitude of foreign lives he has embodied, the more detached and serene he can remain toward them all.
Eventually, the hour arrives when he must retire from the stage and vanish from public view.
The entire sum of what he has lived rises up before his eyes.
He sees the totality of his existence with radical clarity.
He senses the poignant, irreplaceable splendor of that ephemeral journey.
He has looked reality in the face, and now he is ready to die.
There are retirement homes for aged actors.
pairs.move: The Retirement Home for Aged Actors. The closing image of Chapter 6 strips away all theatrical glamour: the retired actor sitting quietly in a rest home. Having lived a hundred intense, contradictory lifetimes, he looks back without illusions. He has exhausted his mortal possibilities and achieved radical clarity; now, having fully expended his life, he can die without regret.
